title: Divisor Subtraction Duel
statement:
Two players share a counter that starts at n. They take turns, and the first player moves first. On a turn the player picks any x with 0 < x < counter that divides the counter evenly, and replaces the counter with counter − x.

A player who has no legal move on their turn loses. Both players play perfectly.

Return true if the first player wins.

examples.why: First takes 1, leaving 3. From 3 the only move is 1, leaving 2. First takes 1, leaving 1, and the second player is stuck.
The only divisor below 3 is 1, so the counter goes 3 → 2 → 1 and the first player is the one stuck at 1.
No x with 0 < x < 1 exists, so the first player cannot move at all.

hints: A position is winning if some move leads to a losing position for the opponent. Work out n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 by hand.
Fill a boolean table win[1..n] from small to large using that rule.
Look at the table: the pattern is about parity. An odd number has only odd divisors, so it always hands the opponent an even number.

explain.intuition:
Classic game DP: a counter value is a win for the player about to move if at least one legal move leaves the opponent in a loss. Value 1 is a loss (no move). Filling the table bottom-up answers any n in about n·√n steps.

The table shows a pattern: even wins, odd loses. Why: from an even number you can always take 1 and hand over an odd number. From an odd number every divisor is odd, and odd minus odd is even, so you always hand over an even number. The player on even stays on even until the other player is stuck at 1.
steps: For each m from 2 to n, try every divisor x < m; if any win[m − x] is false, set win[m] = true.
Or, after spotting the pattern, return n % 2 === 0.
pitfalls: Letting x equal the counter itself. That would jump to 0, which the rules forbid.
Marking a position as winning when all moves lead to wins for the opponent. You need just one move into a losing position.
Guessing the parity rule without the argument behind it. In an interview, show the table or explain why odd numbers only have odd divisors.

complexity.time: O(1) with the parity rule; O(n√n) for the table

solutions.title: Bottom-up win table
solutions.idea: win[m] is true if some divisor x of m (x < m) leaves the opponent at a losing value m − x.

solutions.title: Parity
solutions.idea: Even counters win: take 1 and pass an odd number. Odd counters have only odd divisors and must pass an even number.

followups: Players may only subtract a prime divisor. Does the parity rule survive? Use the table to find out.
Return the number of winning first moves, not just whether one exists.
